title: Rapid Onramp: SDK auth & env setup for Raptor Stack
topics: Auth options (API keys, KMS, Workload Identity)
summary: AE+SE walked Raptor Stack through Redwood SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, focusing on auth patterns (API key, cloud KMS, GCP workload identity), sandbox provisioning, and Console/Optimize basics. Customer raised questions about data residency, KMS integration, CI secret rotation, and latency tradeoffs for dedicated vs hosted. Agreed to provide security pack, a sandbox tenant, and a 1-week benchmark runbook.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-28 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Recording: (available in CRM)

[00:00] Maya Cohen: hey everyone, welcome, thanks for carving out the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, account exec on this account. we've got Diego from solutions engineering with me.
[00:08] Diego Ruiz: hi, thanks for having us. quick agenda — we'll do a 15 minute live SDK quickstart (python + ts), show auth options and the Console to provision a sandbox, then discuss Optimize tips and pilot criteria.
[00:18] Asha Patel: sounds good. we're mainly worried about auth and keys, plus whether we should go hosted or request Dedicated.
[00:22] Jon Murthy: and we want to validate latency under our 300ms p50 target for short prompts.
[00:26] Maya: perfect. okay Diego, take it away for the quickstart.

[02:05] Diego: all right i'll share my screen — ok pulled up the quickstart repo. first file is the python snippet, pip install redwood-sdk (note: in transcript it sometimes shows redwood-client but package is redwood-sdk). so the pattern is super tiny: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, client = Redwood(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']), client.generate(...)
[02:36] Lena Kim: is that auth key scoped? we don't want a single root key.
[02:40] Diego: yes you can create scoped keys in the Console — token-level scopes, expiration, and route restrictions. best practice is to create a low-priv token for the sandbox and rotate it in CI.
[03:01] Jon: what's rotation look like in CI? we use GitHub Actions.
[03:07] Diego: we recommend storing secrets in your cloud KMS (GCP KMS / AWS KMS) or GitHub Secrets if short lived. we have docs for workload identity for GCP so you can avoid long-live keys — the SDK supports ephemeral credentials via workload identity federation.
[03:30] Samir: does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[03:33] Maya: yes, Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) via KMS/HSM integrations; we surface that in the Console under Keys -> External KMS. logs show envelope encryption. we also ship audit logs.

[05:12] Diego: switching to the TypeScript snippet now. npm i @redwood/inference (again, minor transcription: some samples call it @redwood-js in older docs), then in code: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.chat.create(...)
[05:32] Taylor: and the SDK supports streaming?
[05:35] Diego: yes both python and ts support event-streaming; we show how to wire it to SSE and websockets in the examples. streaming is recommended for UX when latency matters.

[07:00] Maya: i'll pause — real quick, on the hosted vs dedicated question: hosted is fastest to get going and cost-per-token is visible in the Console; Dedicated (reserved capacity) gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency for heavy constant traffic. many teams start hosted with a reserved burst and then move to Dedicated once they have steady traffic.
[07:30] Asha: ok but what about data residency/regulatory? we need logs not leaving EU.
[07:38] Maya: we have region pinning for hosted (EU region), and Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) for stricter data residency. for EU-only audit tails we'd recommend Private or Dedicated in an EU region.

[09:05] Diego: back to code — next section is auth via GCP Workload Identity. example shows setting up a service account, mapping to Redwood role in the Console, then using ADC to fetch short-lived creds. snippet: client = Redwood.from_gcp_workload(...). small note: the transcript sometimes captures "workload iden- tity" as "workload identityy" but the idea is the same.
[09:42] Jon: any extra network setup for Workload Identity?
[09:45] Diego: no, that's mostly IAM mapping. for VPC/private deployments you may need direct peering or PrivateLink — we have a guide.

[11:12] Lena: show us the Console?
[11:15] Maya: yeah let me jump to the Console — here's Projects -> sandbox -> API keys, here you can set scopes, expiration, and restrict by route or IP. under Keys we also have KMS bindings.
[12:00] Maya: note the Optimize tab — we provide batching and caching recommendations based on observed traffic patterns. you can upload a sample of prompts and we'll suggest a batching window and KV cache hints.
[12:25] Taylor: is there an automated quantization recommendation?
[12:28] Diego: yes Optimize suggests quantization profiles for models per workload; it's not forceful — it's a guidance table plus estimated cost savings and expected quality delta.

[13:40] Maya: customer question — what's the simplest sandbox route for your team to test?
[13:45] Asha: minimal setup, we want to run black-box latency tests and a handful of prompt sets.
[13:50] Diego: fastest path: we'll provision a sandbox tenant for you with an API scope limited token, example python/ts repo pre-configured, and a small benchmark harness (curl + k6 scripts). you run the 1-week benchmark and we help analyze.

[15:20] Jon: about latency — you mentioned tail latency. our prompts are short (50-150 tokens), mostly server-side. what's the expected p95 difference hosted vs dedicated?
[15:30] Diego: ballpark: hosted p50 might be 80-120ms on small models, p95 could be 400-700ms depending on multi-tenant load. Dedicated can cut p95 by 2-4x because of pinned GPU pools and predictable batching. but this depends on model and seq len.
[16:02] Samir: what about batching — wont batching increase latency?
[16:07] Diego: yes naive batching raises latency for single requests; Redwood's continuous batching and latency-SLO aware policies try to keep latency in-range while using batching for throughput. Optimize will suggest batch size windows per route.

[18:00] Maya: right now let's walkthrough a TypeScript example that uses streaming and the Console provisioned key. Diego, can you run the quick live demo?
[18:10] Diego: running local ts app — hitting the sandbox endpoint with a scoped key — response streaming in, small artifacts in console. (background keyboard noise)
[19:02] Transcript note: some proper nouns misheard — e.g. "KV cache" sometimes captured as "KV cash"

[21:15] Lena: security — we need SOC 2 stuff, encryption at rest, audit logs, and SSO.
[21:22] Maya: we are SOC 2 Type II certified (note: check latest cert in the security pack we'll send). we support SSO via SAML/SCIM provisioning, RBAC in Console, and audit logs export to your SIEM. for KMS: customer-managed keys supported.
[22:10] Asha: we'd like the SOC attestation and a network diagram. can you send that?
[22:14] Maya: yes — action item: we'll send the security pack + network diagram and BYOK guide.

[23:55] Diego: small deep-dive: on the runtime side, if you need ultra-low tail latency we can recommend model variants, sequence length capping, and quantization profiles. also for production we recommend prefix caching for repeated prompts. we have some built-in KV cache helpers in the SDK (example in python quickstart).
[24:30] Jon: how do we measure quality regressions if we change quantization?
[24:33] Diego: Optimize also hooks to evals — you can run A/B on a labeled prompt set; warnings and regression alerts can be configured on your eval suite.

[26:00] Taylor: any gotchas with envs and multi-tenant CI? we have multiple non-prod and prod accounts.
[26:06] Diego: common pattern: per-environment token (sandbox/nonprod/prod) with separate scopes; rotate tokens through CI using the KMS and short lived tokens for deploy jobs. for cross-account we recommend workload identity federation.

[28:12] Maya: let's talk pilot success criteria — what would make this a "go" for you in 30 days?
[28:16] Asha: pass a latency benchmark under p50 200ms and p95 under 450ms for our short prompts; deterministic billing estimates (cost per 1k requests) and security docs delivered.
[28:28] Jon: plus an integration that runs in our staging CI with secret rotation automated.

[29:02] Diego: we can commit to the sandbox + 1-week benchmark and produce a runbook for the tests.

[32:10] Maya: objections — competitor questioning: we heard you talk to OtherCloudAI; can you say what's standing out for you?
[32:17] Asha: OtherCloudAI pushes lower sticker price but less control over on-prem/vpc options. EdgeServe pitched a local runtime but their ops overhead looked higher. so we want a middle ground: easy API + option to go private.
[32:40] Maya: that's exactly the unified inference pitch: same API across hosted/dedicated/private.

[34:05] Diego: quick note on observability: Console exposes per-route token cost, token-level latency, request traces, and a metrics export. we can set up alerting for quality/regression.

[36:00] Taylor: what about secrets scanning in our repo? any recommendations for preventing accidental commit of REDWOOD_API_KEY?
[36:06] Diego: best practice: enforce pre-commit hooks, GitHub geo-coded secrets scanner, plus CI step that rejects long-lived tokens based on scope. we'll include our sample pre-commit config in the repo.

[38:20] Maya: wrapping up, here are the next steps.
[38:25] Maya: 1) we'll provision a sandbox tenant and create a scoped token with expire in 7 days.
[38:30] Maya: 2) send security pack (SOC 2, network diagram, BYOK guide).
[38:34] Maya: 3) share the python + ts quickstart repo and k6 benchmark scripts.
[38:38] Maya: 4) schedule a follow-up check-in after the benchmark to go over results and cadence for Dedicated discussion.

[39:05] Asha: that works. can we get a contact for technical escalation?
[39:08] Maya: Diego will be the SE lead, and I'll own the account.

[40:15] Jon: any cost ballpark for pilot?
[40:19] Maya: for a small sandbox + 1-week benchmark we usually comp the first 2k tokens and provide discounted pilot rates; we'll send a cost estimate in the follow-up.

[42:30] Samir: internal ops question — how are logs exported?
[42:33] Diego: we can stream audit logs to your SIEM via webhook or cloud logging sink (we support BigQuery / Cloud Logging, CloudWatch, and S3 natively).

[44:00] Maya: ok final recap — security pack + sandbox + quickstart repo + benchmark harness + follow-up meeting. Shawn from procurement will join the follow-up if needed.
[44:12] Taylor: thanks everyone.
[44:20] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and next steps.

[47:00] End of recording.

Notes: transcript has typical ASR imperfections; names or product nicknames may be slightly mis-transcribed. References to SDK package names should be validated against the repo (we will link the canonical quickstart in the follow-up).
